text:
Okay, thanks. I found Q3 quite difficult – balancing privacy with helping students is tough. Specifically, deciding on 'small', 'moderate' or 'large' improvements felt arbitrary without knowing *how much* benefit each data source truly adds.

I think questions about explainability (Q4) are crucial. As someone who restarted a degree, I know things can go wrong even with good intentions – clear explanations build trust. 

It’s interesting almost everyone said ‘never’ to age, gender and race/ethnicity. I did too, but it highlights how sensitive that data is. Perhaps an opt-out system could address anxieties around those factors if someone *wanted* to share them for fairness reasons? We need clear boundaries about what's used and why.

I agree with S1 – Q3 felt very abstract. ‘Small’, ‘moderate’… it’s hard to weigh potential benefit against privacy without knowing *what* those improvements actually look like in practice. Especially regarding Absalon data (Q3.4), I worry about creating a surveillance culture, even if the intention is good.

For me, Q5 – fairness versus accuracy – is vital. As an international student who restarted her studies, I’m acutely aware of systemic biases. Losing some overall accuracy to ensure fairer outcomes feels right. 

I was surprised by the strong ‘never’ responses to sensitive data (Q3.5). While I agree with that generally, offering a clear opt-in, with detailed explanation *and* guarantees about how it's used, might address those concerns – but only if truly robust safeguards are in place.

Thanks both of you. I agree with S1 and S6 about Q3 being difficult – those percentages felt really arbitrary. It’s hard to imagine what a “moderate” improvement actually *means* for identifying students who are struggling.

I think the explainability questions (Q4) are super important, especially as an international student still adjusting to how things work here. A lack of transparency would make me very uncomfortable. I answered ‘small’ for high explainability because even a small dip in accuracy felt worth it for understanding *why* a decision was made. 

I also agree with the strong stance on sensitive data, though the idea of a carefully managed opt-in, as S6 mentioned, is interesting – provided there's rock-solid protection and control for students. The group’s answers largely aligned with mine, which I think reflects that we all value privacy highly.

Thanks to everyone who spoke before me – I completely agree about Q3 being difficult. As an advisor, those percentages feel very detached from the students I work with. We need more concrete examples of what each level of improvement actually *looks* like in terms of identifying at-risk students.

I think Q4, explainability, is absolutely key. Students – and frankly, advisors too! – need to understand the reasoning behind any flag. It's about trust and ensuring we’re offering appropriate support. 

I also strongly align with the “never” answers for age, gender and race/ethnicity, but appreciate the opt-in idea raised by S6 - if *students* choose to share that information for fairness purposes, it’s different. Perhaps a separate process, entirely controlled by them? The consistency on those questions is reassuring.

Thanks everyone. I found Q3 really tricky – quantifying improvement feels impossible without knowing the real-world impact. As someone who’s dropped out and restarted, I worry about false positives being *more* damaging than missing some students. The Absalon data (Q3.4) felt particularly invasive; even with assurances it raises red flags for me.

I strongly agree explainability is paramount (Q4). My ADHD makes planning difficult - a 'black box' system wouldn’t help, it would just add stress. I answered ‘small’ across the board because understanding *why* is more important than catching every case. 

The consistent “never” on sensitive data resonates – and the opt-in idea is interesting, but the bar for trust needs to be incredibly high. Maybe a completely separate system for voluntarily sharing that info, not linked to the predictive model itself?

Thanks everyone. I agree with a lot of what’s been said – Q3 was frustratingly abstract. As someone with dyslexia, needing extra time and support already, those percentages felt detached from real student experiences. It's hard to weigh ‘moderate improvement’ against potential overreach.

I think explainability (Q4) is *especially* important for students like me who rely on clear communication. I answered ‘small’ consistently - understanding the 'why' outweighs a small dip in accuracy. 

The strong stance against sensitive data (Q3.5) aligns with my concerns, but the opt-in idea feels worthwhile if rigorously protected – maybe even linked to accessing specific accommodations? The suggestion of a separate system for that data, as S4 mentioned, seems sensible; keep it truly voluntary and distinct.

Thanks everyone. I agree Q3 was difficult – those percentage improvements feel very detached from reality. As someone managing a chronic condition *and* using disability support services, I worry about being flagged due to reduced course load and how that might be misinterpreted. It’s crucial this isn't seen as ‘struggling’, but proactive management of my health.

I strongly agree explainability (Q4) is vital; transparency builds trust when you’re dealing with health issues. I answered “small” consistently - understanding *why* the model flagged something is essential for me to engage meaningfully with support. 

The firm stance against sensitive data resonates, but the opt-in idea, especially linked to accessing accommodations like mine, could be worthwhile – as long as it’s entirely separate and under my control.

Thanks everyone. I agree with a lot of what's been said - Q3 *was* frustratingly abstract. As an advisor for eleven years, those percentage improvements don’t map easily onto actual student situations. We need clearer, practical examples.

I think explainability (Q4) is critical. Students need to understand why they've been flagged so we can have a constructive conversation and offer *targeted* support - not just generic advice. I answered ‘small’ across the board; even a small accuracy loss is worthwhile for that clarity. 

The strong opposition to sensitive data aligns with my ethical concerns, but an opt-in, particularly connected to existing support services like disability accommodations, could be valuable – if handled *very* carefully and entirely separately from the core model. The resource implications of increased contact are a key concern though; we need adequate advisor time.

Thanks everyone. I agree with a lot of what’s been said – Q3 *was* hard to answer. As an international student funding my studies part-time, those percentage improvements felt very distant from my daily reality. The Absalon data especially worried me; it feels like constant monitoring.

I think explainability (Q4) is vital – a lack of transparency would be deeply concerning. I consistently answered “small” because understanding *why* the model made a decision matters more than simply identifying more students. 

The strong stance against sensitive data aligns with my concerns, but an opt-in, if truly voluntary and separate, might be acceptable. It’s reassuring to see so much agreement on that - protecting privacy is clearly paramount here.

Thanks everyone – a really insightful discussion! I agree with many points already made, particularly about Q3 feeling abstract and those percentages being hard to translate into meaningful support for students. As an advisor, seeing concrete examples of what each improvement level *looks like* in practice would be hugely helpful.

I think explainability (Q4) is absolutely crucial – we need to build trust with students. I answered ‘small’ consistently; understanding the reasoning behind a flag allows us to have productive conversations and offer targeted help. 

The strong consensus on avoiding sensitive data is reassuring, but the opt-in idea linked to existing support services *could* work if entirely separate and student-controlled – it's about empowering students with agency over their own data. My biggest concern remains resource constraints; increased outreach requires adequate advisor time.

Thanks everyone, really insightful points. I agree Q3 was incredibly abstract – those percentages felt meaningless without knowing what they *mean* for a student’s life. Having dropped out and restarted, I know getting flagged can be stressful, even if it's well-intentioned.

Explainability (Q4) is vital; clear explanations would have helped me understand things when I was struggling before. My answers reflected that – small improvements are worth the transparency. 

I also strongly agree with the “never” on sensitive data, but the opt-in suggestion tied to accommodations makes sense *if* it’s genuinely separate and under my control. Knowing my past dropout might influence this model is unsettling; separating that context feels crucial for fairness.

Thanks everyone – a really thoughtful discussion! I completely agree with S3 and A2 about Q3 feeling abstract; those percentages are hard to grasp when you're dealing with real students’ lives. As a final-year Masters student struggling with a long-term mental health condition, the idea of being flagged feels… vulnerable.

I think explainability (Q4) is incredibly important – transparency builds trust, especially for someone managing chronic illness. I answered ‘small’ consistently; understanding *why* something triggered a flag allows me to proactively address it and seek support on my terms. 

The strong stance against sensitive data resonates deeply with me; privacy feels paramount. The opt-in idea linked to accommodations is interesting, but only if completely separate – I need absolute control over that information.
